title: Stri: Gandhari's curse
hook: the queen who chose not to see is given sight, and the first thing she sees is the battlefield

segments.voice: Yesterday in Stri, Gandhari held back her curse, and only one glance through her blindfold escaped. Your line was that's all the burning there is. Did you let a breath go by before something sharp? Today, she sees. Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

For years Gandhari has lived behind a cloth she tied on herself. Now the sage Vyasa gives her what the text calls a celestial sight, a way to see far beyond where she stands. She doesn't use it to look at the sky, or at the palace, or at the faces of the Pandavas. She turns it on the field of Kurukshetra, where the war just ended. And standing beside her is Krishna, the one person she will speak to about all of it. Today, what Gandhari sees, and the women she sees there.
screen: `A CLOTH SHE TIED HERSELF.` → `VYASA GIVES HER SIGHT.` → `SHE LOOKS AT THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: What she sees first isn't warriors. It's women. Wives, mothers and daughters of both armies, moving across the field, searching. Some have never walked outside the women's quarters before, and now they're out among the dead, hair loose, calling names. Gandhari describes it all to Krishna, one scene after another. Stri means woman, and here the epic hands the women the story. She sees Uttara, the young widow of Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son, bending over him and talking to him as if he could still hear. She sees her own daughter, Duhshala, running here and there, looking for her husband Jayadratha and unable to find his head. She sees her son Duryodhana lying on the ground, and his wife beside him. She sees Karna, and the women grieving him too. And she keeps turning to Krishna. Look at this, she says. Look at her. Notice what she's doing. Through all of it, she isn't counting victories or losses for one side. The women she describes come from both camps, and their grief sounds the same. A Pandava widow and a Kaurava widow, in this book, are doing exactly the same thing in the dust. The war books spent chapter after chapter on who killed whom. Stri spends its time on who's left to bury them. Grief has been building in Gandhari all this time, and it will break by the end of her speech. But that's tomorrow. Today she simply looks, and makes Krishna look with her.
screen: `SHE SEES THE WOMEN FIRST` · `UTTARA, DUHSHALA, DURYODHANA'S WIFE` · `GRIEF FROM BOTH CAMPS` · then, large: `"LOOK, KRISHNA"`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your eyes rest open, soft, looking at nothing in particular. Bring to mind a conflict you know, near or far, in your family or in the news. Now leave the people who fought it to one side, and look instead at the people who were left afterward on each side. Breathe in, and let one of them come into view. Breathe out, and let one from the other side come into view. Just look. If you pray, you can hold both of them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Stri. Woman. The book where the women of both sides walk onto the field, and Gandhari makes Krishna look at them.
Your line: look at this, she says. Today, when you hear about a fight, ask who's left cleaning up after it. Tomorrow, Gandhari's grief turns on Krishna. Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Gandhari's lament on the battlefield, spoken to Krishna, is read and retold as a passage of mourning, and some modern plays and poems take it up.

fork.setup: you're Gandhari. after years behind a cloth, you can suddenly see far. where do you look?
options: at the faces of the Pandavas.
fork.reveal: she looks at the field, and describes to Krishna the women searching for their dead.

original.note: divine eye: the far sight Vyasa grants, as he once granted it to Sanjaya.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Mahabharata is a story about warriors.
what it means: after the war, a whole book turns to the women left on the field.
what a scholar hears: Gandhari's lament treats the widows of both sides as one grief, which some readers take as the epic's own judgment on the war.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Stri Parva, Gandhari's celestial sight and her lament to Krishna over the battlefield

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm that Vyasa grants Gandhari celestial sight in Ganguli's Stri Parva and that she describes the field to Krishna.
Confirm the scenes named: Uttara over Abhimanyu, Duhshala searching for Jayadratha's head, Duryodhana's wife, and the women grieving Karna.
'Some have never walked outside the women's quarters before' paraphrases the text's description of royal women now seen in public; confirm.
Original word दिव्यचक्षु and the link to Sanjaya's sight: confirm the form and whether the Stri Parva uses this term for Gandhari's sight.
